claim: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of selected experiments from a number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of selected experiments from a number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the purpose and scope of the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology.

claim: The papers selected for replication were published between 2010 and 2012.
source: The papers, which were published between 2010 and 2012, were selected on the basis of citations and Altmetric scores (Errington et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Errington et al., 2014.

claim: The papers selected for replication were chosen on the basis of citations and Altmetric scores.
source: The papers, which were published between 2010 and 2012, were selected on the basis of citations and Altmetric scores (Errington et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Errington et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 are found in gliomas.
source: Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 are found in gliomas and in acute myeloid leukemia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 are found in acute myeloid leukemia.
source: Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 are found in gliomas and in acute myeloid leukemia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: All mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 are heterozygous.
source: All mutations are heterozygous and result in changes to one of two amino acids: arginine 132 in IDH1, or either arginine 172 or arginine 140 in IHD2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mutations in IDH1 result in changes to arginine 132.
source: All mutations are heterozygous and result in changes to one of two amino acids: arginine 132 in IDH1, or either arginine 172 or arginine 140 in IHD2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mutations in IDH2 result in changes to either arginine 172 or arginine 140.
source: All mutations are heterozygous and result in changes to one of two amino acids: arginine 132 in IDH1, or either arginine 172 or arginine 140 in IHD2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Wild-type IDH1 catalyzes the conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate (α-KG).
source: Wild-type IDH1 catalyzes the conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate (α-KG).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The arginine mutations abolish IDH1's normal activity.
source: The arginine mutations abolish its normal activity and instead mutant IDH1 and IDH2 reduce α-KG to generate the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (Ward et al., 2010), which in turn affects the function of multiple α-KG dependent dioxygenases, including the TET family of 5-methylcytosine (5 mC) hydroxylases (Kinney and Pradhan, 2012; McKenney and Levine, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ward et al., 2010, Kinney and Pradhan, 2012, and McKenney and Levine, 2013.

claim: Mutant IDH1 and IDH2 reduce α-KG to generate the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG).
source: The arginine mutations abolish its normal activity and instead mutant IDH1 and IDH2 reduce α-KG to generate the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (Ward et al., 2010), which in turn affects the function of multiple α-KG dependent dioxygenases, including the TET family of 5-methylcytosine (5 mC) hydroxylases (Kinney and Pradhan, 2012; McKenney and Levine, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ward et al., 2010.

claim: 2-HG affects the function of multiple α-KG dependent dioxygenases, including the TET family of 5-methylcytosine (5 mC) hydroxylases.
source: The arginine mutations abolish its normal activity and instead mutant IDH1 and IDH2 reduce α-KG to generate the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) (Ward et al., 2010), which in turn affects the function of multiple α-KG dependent dioxygenases, including the TET family of 5-methylcytosine (5 mC) hydroxylases (Kinney and Pradhan, 2012; McKenney and Levine, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kinney and Pradhan, 2012, and McKenney and Levine, 2013.

claim: Xu and colleagues showed that 2-HG could act as a competitive inhibitor for α-KG-dependent DNA demethylases, specifically Tet2.
source: They showed that 2-HG could act as a competitive inhibitor for α-KG-dependent DNA demethylases, specifically Tet2.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Ectopic expression of the mutant forms of IDH1 and IDH2 inhibited histone demethylation.
source: Ectopic expression of the mutant forms of IDH1 and IDH2 inhibited histone demethylation and 5mC hydroxylation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Ectopic expression of the mutant forms of IDH1 and IDH2 inhibited 5mC hydroxylation.
source: Ectopic expression of the mutant forms of IDH1 and IDH2 inhibited histone demethylation and 5mC hydroxylation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations in IDH1 were associated with increased histone methylation in glioma samples from patients.
source: Examination of glioma samples from patients also showed that mutations in IDH1 were associated with increased histone methylation and decreased 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) levels (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations in IDH1 were associated with decreased 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) levels in glioma samples from patients.
source: Examination of glioma samples from patients also showed that mutations in IDH1 were associated with increased histone methylation and decreased 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) levels (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Transfection of U-87 MG cells with the mutant IDH1R132H increased the amount of 2-HG in the cells, as compared to transfection with wild-type IDH1.
source: In Supplemental Figure 3I, Xu and colleagues demonstrated that transfection of U-87 MG cells with the mutant IDH1R132H increased the amount of 2-HG in the cells, as compared to transfection with wild-type IDH1 (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Supplemental Figure 3I.

claim: 2-HG can occupy the same binding pocket as α-KG in Caenorhabditis elegans KDM7A.
source: Xu and colleagues first showed that 2-HG can occupy the same binding pocket as α-KG in Caenorhabditis elegans KDM7A, indicating it acts as a competitive inhibitor of α-KG.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Xu et al., 2011.

claim: 2-HG acts as a competitive inhibitor of α-KG.
source: Xu and colleagues first showed that 2-HG can occupy the same binding pocket as α-KG in Caenorhabditis elegans KDM7A, indicating it acts as a competitive inhibitor of α-KG.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding pocket data and stated explicitly in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of U-87 MG cells with increasing amounts of 2-HG led to increases in H3K9me2 and H3K79me2.
source: In Figure 3A, they treated U-87 MG cells with cell permeable versions of α-KG and 2-HG, and examined levels of histone methylation by Western Blot. Treatment with increasing amounts of 2-HG led to increases in H3K9me2 and H3K79me2, consistent with the idea that 2-HG inhibited histone demethylases.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The effect of 2-HG on H3K9me2 and H3K79me2 was abolished by co-treatment with α-KG.
source: This effect was abolished by co-treatment with α-KG, confirming a competitive relationship between the two metabolites (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: α-KG and 2-HG have a competitive relationship.
source: This effect was abolished by co-treatment with α-KG, confirming a competitive relationship between the two metabolites (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-treatment experiment and stated explicitly in the manuscript.

claim: Adding increasing concentrations of 2-HG abolished the ability of TET2 to convert 5 mC to 5hmC in an in vitro system.
source: Xu and colleagues also examined the effect of 2-HG on the TET family of 5 mC hydroxylases using an in vitro system of purified TET2 and double-stranded oligos containing a 5mC restriction digestion site in Figure 8A. Adding increasing concentrations of 2-HG abolished the ability of TET2 to convert 5 mC to 5hmC (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 8A.

claim: Transfection of U-87 MG cells with IDH1R132H increased histone methylation.
source: In Figure 3D, they transfected U-87 MG cells with IDH1R132H and assessed levels of histone methylation by Western blot. Transfection with IDH1R132H increased histone methylation, and treatment with α-KG abolished this increase in histone methylation, consistent with the idea that α-KG and 2-HG are competitive metabolites (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with α-KG abolished the increase in histone methylation caused by IDH1R132H transfection.
source: In Figure 3D, they transfected U-87 MG cells with IDH1R132H and assessed levels of histone methylation by Western blot. Transfection with IDH1R132H increased histone methylation, and treatment with α-KG abolished this increase in histone methylation, consistent with the idea that α-KG and 2-HG are competitive metabolites (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: 5hmC levels are normally undetectable in HEK293 cells.
source: In Figure 7B, they also examined TET activity in the presence of mutant IDH1. While 5hmC levels are normally undetectable in HEK293 cells, transfection with TET catalytic domain (CD)-expressing plasmids increased 5hmC levels to detectable amounts.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Transfection with TET catalytic domain (CD)-expressing plasmids increased 5hmC levels to detectable amounts in HEK293 cells.
source: In Figure 7B, they also examined TET activity in the presence of mutant IDH1. While 5hmC levels are normally undetectable in HEK293 cells, transfection with TET catalytic domain (CD)-expressing plasmids increased 5hmC levels to detectable amounts.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Co-transfection of TET-CD and wild-type IDH1 or IDH2 increased levels of 5hmC in HEK293 cells.
source: Co-transfection of TET-CD and wild-type IDH1 or IDH2 increased levels of 5hmC, as expected, while co-transfection of TET-CD with mutant forms of IDH1 and IDH2 decreased 5hmC levels (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Co-transfection of TET-CD with mutant forms of IDH1 and IDH2 decreased 5hmC levels in HEK293 cells.
source: Co-transfection of TET-CD and wild-type IDH1 or IDH2 increased levels of 5hmC, as expected, while co-transfection of TET-CD with mutant forms of IDH1 and IDH2 decreased 5hmC levels (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Lu and colleagues demonstrated that mutations in IDH2 generated abnormal levels of 2-HG which correlated with increased global methylation levels.
source: Using a different cell line than Xu and colleagues, Lu and colleagues demonstrated that mutations in IDH2, similar to mutations in IDH1, also generated abnormal levels of 2-HG which correlated with increased global methylation levels (Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2012.

claim: Expression of exogenous mutated IDH genes in immortalized human cancer cell lines or in erythroid progenitor cells caused increased production of 2HG and increased levels of methylation.
source: Kernystsky and colleagues, Duncan and colleagues and Turcan and colleague have also shown that expression of exogenous mutated IDH genes in immortalized human cancer cell lines or in erythroid progenitor cells caused increased production of 2HG and increased levels of methylation (Duncan et al., 2012; Turcan et al., 2012; Kernytsky et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Duncan et al., 2012; Turcan et al., 2012; Kernytsky et al., 2015.

claim: Conditional knock-in IDH1 mutant mice displayed elevated serum levels of 2HG.
source: Sasaki and colleagues extended these inquiries by generating conditional knock-in IDH1 mutant mice. These mice displayed elevated serum levels of 2HG and similar patterns of hypermethylation as observed in AML patients (Sasaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2012.

claim: Conditional knock-in IDH1 mutant mice displayed similar patterns of hypermethylation as observed in AML patients.
source: Sasaki and colleagues extended these inquiries by generating conditional knock-in IDH1 mutant mice. These mice displayed elevated serum levels of 2HG and similar patterns of hypermethylation as observed in AML patients (Sasaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sasaki et al., 2012.

claim: IDH2 mutant mice displayed an increase in global methylation in heart tissue.
source: Akbay and colleagues generated IDH2 mutant mice and also observed an increase in global methylation in heart tissue.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Akbay et al., 2014.

claim: Mice carrying IDH mutant xenograft tumors displayed higher serum levels of 2HG.
source: They also demonstrated that mice carrying IDH mutant xenograft tumors displayed higher serum levels of 2HG (Akbay et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Akbay et al., 2014.

claim: 2-HG production has been associated with MYC activation in some breast cancers.
source: Recently, 2-HG production has also been associated with MYC activation in some breast cancers, which also displayed increased levels of methylation as compared to tumors with lower levels of 2-HG (Terunuma et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Terunuma et al., 2013.

claim: Breast cancers with MYC activation displayed increased levels of methylation as compared to tumors with lower levels of 2-HG.
source: Recently, 2-HG production has also been associated with MYC activation in some breast cancers, which also displayed increased levels of methylation as compared to tumors with lower levels of 2-HG (Terunuma et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Terunuma et al., 2013.
